Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 53
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Photographer
  trauma_type: Captivity
  pcl5: 62

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Reassurance Seeking: I keep asking others to reassure me that I am okay, Hypervigilance towards people: vigilant for dangerous people, Escape Route Planning: always plan an escape route before entering a place
  Threat: Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard

Vignette:
Mateo had always seen the world through a lens, finding beauty and story in the arrangement of light and shadow. At fifty-three, his portfolio was a testament to a life spent chasing those moments, from bustling cityscapes to remote, forgotten landscapes. That life, however, felt like it belonged to another man. The turning point was an assignment eighteen months ago, documenting the work of a small aid organization in a region destabilized by conflict. He remembers the dust, the heat, the sudden stop of the jeep. He remembers the rough texture of the hood they threw over his head more than the faces of the men who took him. For nine days, his world shrank to the size of a small, windowless room. His captors were unpredictable; their presence was announced by the scrape of a metal bolt, their intentions by the speed and violence of their movements. A hand reaching for a water bottle could just as easily become a sudden, brutal shove. He learned to read the shifts in their weight, the cadence of their footsteps, living in a state of suspended terror, a spring coiled so tightly he thought his own muscles might snap.

Since his release and return home, the coil has never fully unwound. His body remains on high alert, a low thrum of adrenaline a constant companion. His shoulders are perpetually tight, his jaw set, ready for an impact that never comes but always feels imminent. The world, once his studio, has become a landscape of potential threats. He finds himself unable to enter a new space—a cafe, a grocery store, even a friend's living room—without first identifying all possible exits. His mind automatically calculates the fastest route from where he is to safety, a habit forged in a place where there was no escape at all. This extends to where he allows himself to be. He will no longer sit in the middle of a restaurant; he must have a booth, his back pressed firmly against a solid wall, the entire room within his field of vision. His wife, Elena, has learned to scan a room for the "safe seat" before even suggesting a table.

His work, his greatest passion, has become a source of profound anxiety. As a photographer, he must move through crowds, yet the unpredictable motion of other people feels like a direct assault. During a wedding reception a few months back, a guest spun around suddenly on the dance floor, and Mateo flinched so violently he dropped a lens. He felt a surge of pure, unreasoning panic, his body screaming danger in a room full of celebration. Since then, he has turned down all event work, confining himself to static studio portraits. The loss of income is a concern, but the loss of his identity as a photographer who moved freely through the world is a deeper wound. He constantly scans the people around him, not for a compelling shot, but for signs of danger. He assesses their posture, the way they hold their hands, the look in their eyes, certain he can spot a threat before it materializes.

This constant threat assessment has eroded his trust in his own perceptions. He finds himself turning to Elena dozens of time a day for confirmation that he is safe. "Does that person look okay to you?" he will whisper in the street. At night, he will ask her repeatedly if the doors are locked, if she heard the same faint noise he did. He knows, logically, that he is home and safe, but the feeling of pervasive danger is so overwhelming that he needs her to be his anchor to reality. It was after one such night, when he woke her for the fourth time to check a lock he had already checked himself, that he saw the exhaustion and fear in her eyes—fear for him. That look is what finally brought him to therapy. He is terrified that the man he was is gone forever, replaced by this watchful, frightened stranger. More than anything, he wants to be able to sit in a cafe with his wife, his back to the door, and think only about the taste of his coffee.
